title: Filesystems in Go
summary: Build a tiny filesystem on an in-memory block device: superblock, block bitmap, inodes, directories, an fsck, and a journal that survives a crash at every write.
description: A filesystem is a data structure that has to stay consistent while the power can fail between any two writes. You build one called BMFS on a simulated block device, one layer per lesson: a superblock, a bitmap that hands out blocks, inodes that own them, directories that name them, and an fsck that finds orphan and duplicate blocks. Then you add a fault-injecting disk that loses every write after a chosen point, see what naive code leaves behind, fix it by ordering writes, and finish with a small write-ahead journal for metadata that is tested at every possible crash position. Everything is deterministic and in memory. The crash model is stated plainly in the lessons: a power cut keeps a prefix of the writes, in order, and every block write is atomic. Real disks are worse, and the lessons say where.
outcomes: Lay out and decode an on-disk format: superblock, bitmap, inode table and directory entries.
Write an fsck that classifies orphan, duplicate and dangling references without panicking on garbage.
Enumerate every crash point of an operation and show which ones leave damage.
Order writes so a crash only leaks space, then add a write-ahead journal that makes metadata updates all-or-nothing.
